questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists only SI base quantities according to the module?
options: Length, electric current, and thermodynamic temperature
Power, amount of substance, and pressure
questions.explanation: Length, mass, time, temperature, electric current, amount of substance, and luminous intensity are the seven fundamental SI base quantities[cite: 12].

questions.question: What is the SI base unit and dimension symbol for amount of substance?
questions.explanation: Table 1.1 states that amount of substance has the unit mole (symbol N) and dimension 1[cite: 12].

questions.question: What is the dimensional formula for pressure in SI units?
questions.explanation: Pressure is defined as force per unit area, yielding the dimension kg · m⁻¹ · s⁻² (Pa)[cite: 12].

questions.question: A vehicle weighs 2,500 lb. What is its equivalent mass in kilograms?
questions.explanation: Using the conversion factor 1 lb = 0.4536 kg: 2500 × 0.4536 kg = 1134.0 kg[cite: 13].

questions.question: Errors that result from measuring devices being out of calibration and cause readings to be consistently too small or too large are called:
questions.explanation: Systematic errors result from measuring devices being out of calibration and can be eliminated by pre-calibrating against a trusted standard[cite: 14].

questions.question: What is the uncertainty in a single reading obtained from an analog scale measuring device such as a meter stick?
options: Equal to the smallest increment divided by 2
Equal to twice the smallest increment
questions.explanation: By the general rule of thumb, the uncertainty in a scale measuring device equals the smallest increment divided by 2[cite: 14].

questions.question: What is the uncertainty associated with a digital balance reading of 5.7513 kg?
questions.explanation: Uncertainty in a digital measuring device equals the smallest increment, which is 0.0001 kg[cite: 15].

questions.question: How many significant figures are in the numbers 0.0062 cm and 4.0500 cm respectively?
questions.explanation: Zeros that do nothing but set the decimal point are not significant (0.0062 has 2), while trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant (4.0500 has 5)[cite: 16, 17].

questions.question: Following the rules for significant figures, what is the result of 9.65 cm + 8.4 cm - 2.89 cm?
questions.explanation: The least precise measurement is 8.4 cm (one decimal place), so the result must be rounded to the nearest tenth: 15.2 cm[cite: 17].

questions.question: What happens to a vector when it is multiplied by a negative pure scalar number?
options: It turns into a dimensionless scalar
Its magnitude changes and its direction is reversed
Its direction stays unchanged but its units change
It automatically becomes a unit vector
questions.explanation: Multiplication by a pure number changes magnitude; if the number is negative, the direction is reversed[cite: 17].

questions.question: Which mathematical law gives the magnitude of the resultant vector R formed by two concurrent vectors A and B with an included angle θ?
questions.explanation: Applying the cosine law to the vector triangle gives R = √(A² + B² - 2AB cos θ)[cite: 18].

questions.question: If a 3D vector A has components Ax, Ay, and Az, what is its magnitude?
questions.explanation: The magnitude of a three-dimensional vector is given by √(Ax² + Ay² + Az²)[cite: 19].

questions.question: What is the direction cosine cos θx for a vector A with respect to the positive x-axis?
questions.explanation: The direction cosine is defined as cos θx = Ax / A[cite: 20].

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes a unit vector?
options: It has a magnitude of 1 unit with dimensions of meters
It has a magnitude of one, is dimensionless, and solely specifies direction
It always points perpendicular to the Cartesian coordinate system
It represents the sum of all scalar quantities in an equation
questions.explanation: A unit vector has a magnitude of one, is dimensionless, and its sole purpose is to specify direction[cite: 20, 22].

questions.question: How is the unit vector û in the direction of vector r⃗ = xî + yĵ + zk̂ calculated?
options: û = r⃗ / r, where r = √(x² + y² + z²)
questions.explanation: The unit vector is obtained by dividing the vector by its magnitude: û = r⃗ / r[cite: 21].

questions.question: Given A⃗ = 3î - 4ĵ + 4k̂ and B⃗ = 2î + 3ĵ - 7k̂, what is the magnitude of A⃗ + B⃗?
What is the SI unit and dimension of power?
questions.explanation: Table 1.2 specifies power as energy per unit time with SI unit watt (W) and dimension kg · m² · s⁻³[cite: 12].

questions.question: If a cat has a body temperature of 101.5°F, what is its temperature in Celsius?
What is the sum of vectors A⃗ = Axî + Ayĵ + Azk̂ and B⃗ = Bxî + Byĵ + Bzk̂ in unit vector notation?
questions.explanation: In unit vector notation, corresponding Cartesian components are added algebraically: (Ax + Bx)î + (Ay + By)ĵ + (Az + Bz)k̂[cite: 21].

questions.question: In the graphical method of vector addition, how is the resultant vector drawn?
options: From the head of the first vector to the tail of the last vector
From the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector
From the midpoint of the first vector to the midpoint of the second
questions.explanation: Graphically, the resultant vector is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head (tip) of the last vector[cite: 18].

questions.question: How are average velocity and average speed fundamentally distinguished?
options: Average velocity is total distance over time; average speed is total displacement over time
Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time; average speed is total path distance divided by elapsed time
There is no distinction; both are identical vector quantities
Average speed is always zero in circular motion while average velocity is non-zero
questions.explanation: Average velocity is Δr⃗ / Δt (displacement over time), whereas average speed is total distance S over time[cite: 26].

questions.question: A person walks along a straight line from A to B at 5 m/s and returns from B to A along the same line at 3 m/s. What are their average speed and average velocity over the entire trip?
options: Average speed = 4.0 m/s; average velocity = 4.0 m/s
Average speed = 3.75 m/s; average velocity = 0 m/s
Average speed = 0 m/s; average velocity = 3.75 m/s
Average speed = 8.0 m/s; average velocity = 2.0 m/s
questions.explanation: Average speed = 2x / (x/5 + x/3) = 15/4 = 3.75 m/s[cite: 27]. Since initial and final positions coincide, net displacement is 0, making average velocity 0 m/s[cite: 27].

questions.question: Which kinematic equation describes the final velocity vf in terms of initial velocity vi, constant acceleration a, and displacement Δr?
questions.explanation: For constant acceleration, vf² = vi² + 2aΔr[cite: 28].

questions.question: A jet lands at 100 m/s and decelerates smoothly at 5 m/s² until it stops. What runway length is required for it to come to rest?
questions.explanation: Time to stop: t = 100 / 5 = 20 s[cite: 29]. Stopping distance: S = ((100 + 0) / 2) × 20 = 1000 m (1.0 km)[cite: 29].

questions.question: In standard ideal projectile motion, what are the horizontal acceleration ax and vertical acceleration ay?
options: ax = u cos θ, ay = u sin θ
questions.explanation: Assuming negligible air resistance, no horizontal force acts (ax = 0), and gravity acts downward (ay = -g)[cite: 32].

questions.question: What is the formula for the maximum height h reached by a projectile launched with speed u at angle θ?
questions.explanation: At maximum height, vy = 0, giving h = (u² sin² θ) / (2g)[cite: 33].

questions.question: At what launch angle θ is the horizontal range of a projectile maximum?
questions.explanation: The range formula R = (u² sin 2θ) / g is maximized when sin 2θ = 1, which occurs at θ = 45°[cite: 33].

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding Newton's third law action-reaction pairs?
options: They act on the same object and cancel each other out to produce zero net force
They exist in pairs, act on different interacting bodies, and cannot cancel each other
The action force occurs before the reaction force
They only exist when objects move with constant acceleration
questions.explanation: Action and reaction forces always exist in pairs and act on different objects; hence they never cancel each other out[cite: 40, 41].

questions.question: How does the coefficient of kinetic friction μk compare to the coefficient of static friction μs between the same surfaces?
options: μk is always greater than μs
μk is generally less than μs
μk equals μs under all loads
questions.explanation: Generally, μk is less than μs, meaning less force is required to keep an object sliding than to start sliding[cite: 42].

questions.question: What is the acceleration of a block of mass m sliding down a frictionless incline tilted at angle θ?
questions.explanation: Along the plane, the net force is mg sin θ = ma, which simplifies to a = g sin θ[cite: 45].

questions.question: In uniform circular motion with constant speed v and radius r, what is the magnitude and direction of acceleration?
options: ac = v / r, tangent to the circular path
ac = v² / r, directed toward the center of the circle
ac = v² / r, directed outward away from the center
questions.explanation: Centripetal acceleration has magnitude ac = v² / r and is directed radially inward toward the center[cite: 46, 47].

questions.question: What is the value of the universal gravitational constant G in SI units?
questions.explanation: The universal gravitational constant G measured experimentally is 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N · m² / kg²[cite: 48].

questions.question: Which of Kepler's laws states that a line connecting the Sun and a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time?
questions.explanation: Kepler's second law is the Law of Areas, which describes the varying orbital speed of a planet[cite: 49, 50].

questions.question: What physical condition creates the true sensation of weightlessness experienced by orbiting astronauts?
options: The complete absence of gravitational force in space
The state of free fall where all contact forces are removed
The presence of an atmospheric vacuum that cancels mass
Zero velocity relative to the Earth's center
questions.explanation: Weightlessness occurs during free fall because no external contact surface supports the body with an opposing normal force[cite: 52].

questions.question: According to Hooke's law, the restoring force Fs exerted by a spring displaced by distance x from equilibrium is:
questions.explanation: Hooke's law states Fs = -kx, where the negative sign indicates the force opposes displacement[cite: 54].

questions.question: What does the work-kinetic energy theorem state?
options: Work done is always equal to total potential energy
The net work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy (Wnet = ΔKE)
Work done is independent of force and displacement
The rate of work done equals linear momentum
questions.explanation: The work-kinetic energy theorem states that Wnet = ΔKE = ½mvf² - ½mvi²[cite: 56, 57].

questions.question: How much energy in joules is represented by one kilowatt-hour (1 kWh)?
How is the impulse I⃗ of a net force F⃗ acting over time interval Δt related to linear momentum P⃗?
options: I⃗ = ΔP⃗ = P⃗f - P⃗i = F⃗ Δt
questions.explanation: Impulse equals the change in linear momentum: I⃗ = ΔP⃗ = F⃗ Δt[cite: 60].

questions.question: A collision in which both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved is classified as:
questions.explanation: An elastic collision is defined as one where both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved[cite: 62].

questions.question: Two particles of masses m1 = 1 kg and m2 = 2 kg are positioned on the x-axis at x1 = 1 m and x2 = 4 m. Where is the center of mass xCM located?
What is the defining characteristic of elastic materials compared to plastic materials?
options: Elastic materials undergo irreversible deformation under any small load
Elastic materials regain their original shape and size when the deforming force is removed
Plastic materials store more strain energy per unit volume than elastic materials
Elastic materials cannot be subjected to tensile stress
questions.explanation: Elastic materials return to their original shape when deforming forces are removed within their elastic limit, whereas plastic materials deform permanently[cite: 72].

questions.question: How are stress and strain defined respectively?
options: Stress is fractional change in length; strain is deforming force per unit area
Stress is force per unit area (N/m²); strain is change in configuration divided by initial configuration (dimensionless)
Both are dimensionless ratios of force to area
Stress is measured in joules; strain is measured in pascals
questions.explanation: Stress is force per unit area (Pa); strain is the fractional deformation and is dimensionless[cite: 72].

questions.question: Which elastic modulus measures the resistance of a solid to a change in its length under tension or compression?
questions.explanation: Young's modulus Y is defined as tensile stress divided by tensile strain and characterizes resistance to length change[cite: 75].

questions.question: Why do liquids have a bulk modulus but no defined Young's modulus or shear modulus?
options: Liquids cannot sustain a shearing or tensile stress and simply flow in response
The bulk modulus of all liquids is strictly zero
Liquids are completely incompressible under all pressures
questions.explanation: Liquids do not have fixed shape or sustain shear/tensile stress; applying a shear force causes them to flow[cite: 76].

questions.question: The reciprocal of the bulk modulus (1/B) is known as:
questions.explanation: Compressibility is defined as the reciprocal of the bulk modulus[cite: 76].

questions.question: What is the specific gravity (SG) of a substance?
options: Its mass per unit volume in g/cm³
The ratio of its density to the density of pure water at 4°C (1.0 × 10³ kg/m³)
Its weight density multiplied by gravitational acceleration
The buoyant force exerted on it when submerged in alcohol
questions.explanation: Specific gravity is a dimensionless ratio comparing the density of a substance to that of water at 4°C[cite: 77].

questions.question: What is the hydrostatic gauge pressure produced at depth h in a static fluid of uniform density ρ?
questions.explanation: The hydrostatic pressure of a fluid column of height h is Pgauge = ρgh[cite: 78].

questions.question: How are absolute pressure, gauge pressure, and atmospheric pressure related?
questions.explanation: Absolute pressure is the sum of gauge pressure and local atmospheric pressure: Pabs = Pgauge + Patm[cite: 79].

questions.question: Pascal's principle states that:
options: The buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid
Pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished to every portion of the fluid and container walls
Swiftly moving fluids exert higher lateral pressure than static fluids
The total mass flux through a tube varies with elevation
questions.explanation: Pascal's principle dictates that an applied pressure change is transmitted undiminished throughout an enclosed fluid[cite: 79, 86].

questions.question: In a hydraulic press, a force F1 is applied to a piston of area A1. What force F2 is produced on a larger piston of area A2?
questions.explanation: Equating pressures P1 = P2 gives F1 / A1 = F2 / A2, so F2 = F1(A2 / A1)[cite: 80].

questions.question: According to Archimedes' principle, what is the magnitude of the buoyant force acting on a submerged body?
options: Equal to the total weight of the submerged body
Equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the body
Equal to atmospheric pressure multiplied by the body surface area
Equal to the difference between Young's modulus and bulk modulus
questions.explanation: Archimedes' principle states that the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid: Fb = ρfluid · Vdisplaced · g[cite: 81].

questions.question: Why does a buoyant force act upward on an object submerged in a fluid?
options: Fluid density decreases at greater depth
Fluid pressure increases with depth, causing the upward force on the bottom to exceed the downward force on the top
Atmospheric pressure pushes the bottom of the container upward
Surface tension pulls the submerged body toward the meniscus
questions.explanation: Because pressure increases with depth, the pressure on the bottom of an object is greater than at its top, resulting in a net upward force[cite: 81].

questions.question: A sample weighs 300 N in air and 200 N when submerged in an alcohol solution of density 700 kg/m³. What is the density of the sample?
questions.explanation: Fb = 300 - 200 = 100 N[cite: 81]. Density ρ0 = ρalcohol × (Wair / Fb) = 700 × (300 / 100) = 2,100 kg/m³[cite: 81].

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption made for an ideal fluid undergoing steady flow?
options: The fluid is non-viscous (no internal friction)
The fluid is compressible (density varies greatly with pressure)
The flow is steady (velocity at each point remains constant in time)
The flow is irrotational (no angular momentum about any point)
questions.explanation: Ideal fluids are assumed to be incompressible (density remains constant)[cite: 82].

questions.question: The equation of continuity for an incompressible fluid flowing through a pipe states that:
questions.explanation: The equation of continuity expresses conservation of mass: volume flow rate Av = A1v1 = A2v2 = constant[cite: 83].

questions.question: What happens to the speed of an ideal fluid when the cross-sectional area of the pipe decreases?
questions.explanation: Because Av = constant, decreasing the area A requires an increase in flow speed v[cite: 83].

questions.question: Bernoulli's equation is a mathematical statement of which fundamental physical principle applied to fluids?
questions.explanation: Bernoulli's equation is derived directly from the work-energy theorem and represents conservation of energy for flowing fluids[cite: 83].

questions.question: According to Bernoulli's principle, what happens to fluid pressure in a horizontal streamline where the fluid velocity increases?
questions.explanation: Bernoulli's principle states that swiftly moving fluids exert lower pressure than slowly moving fluids[cite: 83].

questions.question: What is the full mathematical statement of Bernoulli's equation for points 1 and 2 along a streamline?
options: P1 + ρv1 + ρgh1 = P2 + ρv2 + ρgh2
P1 + ½ρv1² + ρgh1 = P2 + ½ρv2² + ρgh2
questions.explanation: Bernoulli's equation is P + ½ρv² + ρgy = constant[cite: 84].

questions.question: A steel bolt has a diameter of 1.00 cm. If its ultimate shear stress is 4.0 × 10⁸ N/m², what shearing force is required to shear the bolt?
questions.explanation: Area = πr² = π(0.005 m)² ≈ 7.854 × 10⁻⁵ m². Force = Stress × Area = (4.0 × 10⁸ N/m²) × (7.854 × 10⁻⁵ m²) ≈ 3.14 × 10⁴ N.

questions.question: The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics establishes the physical basis for:
options: The concept and measurement of temperature
The impossibility of reaching absolute zero
The direction of spontaneous heat flow
questions.explanation: The Zeroth law states that if objects A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, they are in equilibrium with each other, defining temperature[cite: 90, 91].

questions.question: What are the freezing and boiling points of pure water on the Fahrenheit scale at standard atmospheric pressure?
questions.explanation: On the Fahrenheit scale, the freezing point of water is 32°F and the boiling point is 212°F[cite: 91].

questions.question: How are the coefficients of linear expansion (α), areal expansion (β), and volume expansion (γ) related for an isotropic solid?
questions.explanation: For isotropic materials, areal expansion β = 2α and volumetric expansion γ = 3α[cite: 93, 104].

questions.question: Why does a bimetallic strip made of brass and steel bend when heated?
options: Brass has a higher coefficient of linear expansion than steel and expands more
The heat melts the bonding solder between the two metals
One metal becomes magnetic upon heating
questions.explanation: Brass expands more than steel due to its higher expansion coefficient (19 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ vs. 12 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹), forcing the strip to bend[cite: 92, 93].

questions.question: How does internal energy U differ from heat Q in thermodynamics?
options: Internal energy is energy in transit; heat is stored microscopic energy
Internal energy is the total random kinetic and potential energy of microscopic constituents; heat is transient energy transferred due to temperature difference
Heat is a state function; internal energy is a path-dependent process
They are completely identical physical quantities
questions.explanation: Internal energy is the stored energy of microscopic molecular motion; heat is only energy in transit across a boundary due to ΔT[cite: 94, 104].

questions.question: The quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C is called its:
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity c is the amount of heat energy needed to raise the temperature of a unit mass of substance by one degree[cite: 95].

questions.question: What is latent heat of fusion (Lf)?
options: Heat needed to raise the temperature of steam by 10°C
Heat absorbed or released per unit mass during a solid-liquid phase transition at constant temperature
Heat required to vaporize a liquid into gas
questions.explanation: Latent heat of fusion is the energy per unit mass required to change matter from solid to liquid at its melting point[cite: 96].

questions.question: What is the mathematical equation for the first law of thermodynamics?
questions.explanation: The module defines the first law as ΔU = Q + W, where W is the work done on the system[cite: 101, 105].

questions.question: In an adiabatic thermodynamic process, which quantity is strictly zero?
questions.explanation: An adiabatic process is one in which no heat energy enters or leaves the system (Q = 0)[cite: 102, 105].

questions.question: In an isochoric (isovolumetric) process, what is the work done W by or on the gas?
questions.explanation: Because volume remains constant (ΔV = 0), no mechanical boundary work is performed: W = 0[cite: 102, 105].

questions.question: What is the change in internal energy (ΔU) of a system undergoing a complete cyclic process?
questions.explanation: Since the system returns to its initial state, its state function U undergoes zero net change: ΔU = 0[cite: 102, 105].

questions.question: How is work done on an ideal gas calculated during an isothermal expansion from volume Vi to Vf at constant temperature T?
questions.explanation: The work done during an isothermal process of an ideal gas is given by W = -nRT ln(Vf / Vi)[cite: 102, 105].

questions.question: Which mechanism of heat transfer occurs through the physical macroscopic movement of fluid particles themselves?
questions.explanation: Convection involves the bulk displacement and circulation of heated fluid molecules[cite: 98, 99].

questions.question: Why does thermal radiation not require any material medium for heat transfer?
options: It travels as electromagnetic waves that can propagate through vacuum
It is driven by acoustic longitudinal phonons
It consists of free electron conduction in metal lattices
It operates through gravitational potential displacement
questions.explanation: Radiation is transmitted in the form of electromagnetic energy waves, allowing it to travel through empty space[cite: 100].

questions.question: How does the intensity of radiant heat energy received from a point source vary with distance r?
options: Inversely proportional to the square of the distance (1/r²)
questions.explanation: Radiant heat energy decreases inversely with the square of the distance from the radiant source[cite: 100].

questions.question: If 2000 J of heat leaves a thermodynamic system and 2500 J of work is done on the system, what is the change in internal energy ΔU?
questions.explanation: Using ΔU = Q + W: Q = -2000 J (leaves system) and W = +2500 J (done on system), so ΔU = -2000 + 2500 = +500 J[cite: 101, 103].

questions.question: The temperature of a 525 g silver bar rises by 10.0°C when it absorbs 1.23 kJ of heat. What is the specific heat of silver?
Why is water extraordinarily effective as an extinguishing agent for structure fires?
options: It has an extremely low latent heat of vaporization
It has a very high specific heat capacity and high heat of vaporization, absorbing massive amounts of heat as it warms and vaporizes
It increases oxygen concentration in burning wood
It reacts chemically to produce non-flammable solid minerals
questions.explanation: Water has an exceptionally high specific heat and latent heat of vaporization, enabling it to absorb vast quantities of heat and cool fuels[cite: 96, 101].

questions.question: Why does a vacuum flask (Thermos bottle) effectively preserve hot liquids?
options: Its double walls reflect magnetic field lines
The vacuum evacuated between the silvered double walls prevents heat loss by both conduction and convection
The flask continuously generates electric current to reheat the fluid
The lid absorbs radiant heat from room air
questions.explanation: A vacuum lacks particles, preventing conduction and convection, while mirrored walls minimize radiative transfer[cite: 99, 100].

questions.question: What is the SI unit of absolute thermodynamic temperature, defined as 1/273.16 of the triple point of water?
questions.explanation: The SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature is the kelvin (K)[cite: 12, 104].

questions.question: What is the defining condition for a system to execute Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)?
options: The acceleration is constant in both magnitude and direction
The restoring force and acceleration are directly proportional to displacement and opposite in direction (a = -ω²x)
The amplitude increases exponentially over time
The motion is non-periodic and purely rotational
questions.explanation: SHM occurs when the restoring force obeys Hooke's law, causing acceleration to be proportional to displacement and directed opposite to it: a = -ω²x[cite: 101, 111].

questions.question: Where do the maximum velocity and maximum acceleration occur in the oscillation cycle of an SHM system?
options: vmax at maximum displacement x = ±A; amax at equilibrium x = 0
vmax at equilibrium position x = 0; amax at maximum displacement x = ±A
Both vmax and amax occur simultaneously at x = 0
Both vmax and amax occur simultaneously at x = A
questions.explanation: Speed is maximum at equilibrium (x = 0, vmax = ωA) and zero at turnarounds; acceleration is maximum at extreme displacements (x = ±A, amax = ω²A)[cite: 112].

questions.question: How does the period T of a simple pendulum of length L depend on the mass m of the bob for small amplitudes?
options: T is directly proportional to m
T is independent of the mass m (T = 2π√(L/g))
questions.explanation: The period formula T = 2π√(L/g) contains no mass term; it depends only on pendulum length and local gravitational acceleration[cite: 114].

questions.question: What is the total mechanical energy of a simple harmonic oscillator of spring constant k and amplitude A?
questions.explanation: Total energy in SHM is constant and proportional to the square of the amplitude: E = ½ kA²[cite: 115].

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between mechanical waves and electromagnetic waves?
options: Mechanical waves can travel through a vacuum, whereas electromagnetic waves require a material medium
Mechanical waves require a physical material medium to propagate, whereas electromagnetic waves can propagate through both a medium and a vacuum
Electromagnetic waves are strictly longitudinal; mechanical waves are always transverse
Mechanical waves travel at the speed of light
questions.explanation: Mechanical waves require a deformable material medium, whereas EM waves consist of oscillating fields that propagate through vacuum at c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s[cite: 116].

questions.question: In a transverse wave, how do the particles of the medium vibrate relative to the direction of wave propagation?
options: Parallel to the direction of wave motion
Perpendicular to the direction of wave motion
In circular orbits opposite to wave velocity
They do not vibrate at all
questions.explanation: In transverse waves, particle displacement is perpendicular (transverse) to the direction of wave propagation[cite: 117].

questions.question: What is the relationship connecting wave speed v, wavelength λ, and frequency f?
questions.explanation: The wave speed equation is v = λf[cite: 116].

questions.question: The phenomenon in which an external driving force matches the natural frequency of an oscillating system, causing a dramatic increase in amplitude, is called:
questions.explanation: Resonance occurs when a periodic force drives an oscillating system at or near its natural frequency, maximizing amplitude[cite: 117].

questions.question: What frequency shift is perceived by a stationary observer when a sound source moves toward them at speed vs?
options: A downward shift to lower frequency
An upward shift to higher frequency: fo = fs [v / (v - vs)]
No shift in frequency, only an increase in amplitude
questions.explanation: Due to the Doppler effect, wave crests are compressed toward an approaching observer, increasing the observed pitch/frequency[cite: 117, 118].

questions.question: The bending or change in direction of a wave as it passes obliquely from one medium to another due to a change in speed is called:
questions.explanation: Refraction is the change in propagation direction resulting from a difference in wave speed between two media[cite: 119].

questions.question: The spreading of waves around the edges of obstacles or through small apertures is termed:
questions.explanation: Diffraction is the bending and spreading of waves around obstacles, most pronounced when obstacle size is comparable to wavelength[cite: 119].

questions.question: What type of image is always formed by a single flat plane mirror?
options: Virtual, erect, same size as the object, and located the same distance behind the mirror
questions.explanation: Plane mirrors always form virtual, erect images that are the same size as the object and situated at an image distance equal to the object distance[cite: 120, 121, 126].

questions.question: Which type of lens is thicker at its center and converges incident parallel light rays to a real focal point?
questions.explanation: Convex lenses are converging lenses that are thickest at the center and converge parallel rays to a real focus[cite: 121, 126].

questions.question: What are the characteristics of images formed by a concave (diverging) lens for any real object position?
questions.explanation: Table 5.2 notes that images formed by a concave lens are always virtual, erect, and diminished[cite: 123, 124].

questions.question: What is the thin lens equation relating object distance so, image distance si, and focal length f?
questions.explanation: The lens equation is 1/so + 1/si = 1/f[cite: 122].

questions.question: When an object is placed at the focal point (F1) of a convex lens, where is the image formed?
questions.explanation: Table 5.1 specifies that an object located at F1 produces refracted parallel rays that form an image at infinity[cite: 122, 123].

questions.question: An object in simple harmonic motion follows x(t) = 4 cos(πt + π/4). What is the angular frequency ω of the motion?
questions.explanation: Comparing with x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), the angular frequency ω multiplying t is π rad/s[cite: 112].

questions.question: What effect does increasing the temperature have on the time kept by a pendulum clock with a metal rod?
options: The rod expands, increasing length L, which increases period T, causing the clock to run slow
The rod contracts, decreasing length L, causing the clock to run fast
Temperature has zero effect on the period
The period decreases because density decreases
questions.explanation: Thermal expansion lengthens the rod (ΔL > 0); since T = 2π√(L/g), the period increases and the clock loses time (runs slow)[cite: 92, 114, 127].

questions.question: The pulsating variation in sound intensity (beats) heard when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies interfere results from:
options: Alternating constructive and destructive interference over time
Doppler shifts in the air molecules
questions.explanation: Beats arise from the superposition of two wave trains with slightly different frequencies, periodically reinforcing and canceling each other[cite: 119, 120].

questions.question: What is the speed of all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum?
questions.explanation: All electromagnetic waves propagate through vacuum at the universal speed of light, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s[cite: 116].

questions.question: What is the elementary charge carried by a single proton or electron?
questions.explanation: The elementary charge magnitude is e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C[cite: 129].

questions.question: According to Coulomb's Law, what is the electrostatic force between two charges q1 and q2 separated by distance r in vacuum?
questions.explanation: Coulomb's law states that the electrostatic force is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to r²[cite: 130].

questions.question: How is the electric field E⃗ at a point defined in terms of the force F⃗ experienced by a small positive test charge q0?
questions.explanation: Electric field is defined as the electrostatic force per unit test charge: E⃗ = F⃗ / q0[cite: 132].

questions.question: Electric field lines around an isolated positive point charge always point:
options: Radially outward away from the charge
In concentric circular loops around the charge
questions.explanation: By convention, electric field lines emanate radially outward from positive charges and terminate on negative charges[cite: 133, 134].

questions.question: What is the electric potential difference (voltage) V between two points?
options: Electric potential energy divided by charge: V = ΔU / q
Force times charge: V = F · q
Current per unit resistance: V = I / R
Work divided by acceleration: V = W / a
questions.explanation: Electric potential difference is defined as change in electric potential energy per unit charge: V = ΔU / q, measured in volts (J/C)[cite: 138].

questions.question: How is electric current I defined in terms of charge flow ΔQ over time interval Δt?
questions.explanation: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge: I = ΔQ / Δt[cite: 140].

questions.question: What is the microscopic form of Ohm's law relating current density J⃗, conductivity σ, and electric field E⃗?
questions.explanation: In microscopic form, Ohm's law is J⃗ = σE⃗, where σ is electrical conductivity[cite: 142].

questions.question: Which formula expresses electric power dissipated in a resistor of resistance R carrying current I under voltage V?
questions.explanation: Electrical power is given by P = IV = I²R = V² / R[cite: 143].

questions.question: Kirchhoff's Junction Rule (ΣIin = ΣIout) is a direct consequence of which conservation law?
questions.explanation: The junction rule states that total current entering a node equals current leaving it, representing conservation of electric charge[cite: 144, 145].

questions.question: Kirchhoff's Loop Rule (ΣV = 0 around any closed circuit loop) is a direct consequence of:
questions.explanation: The loop rule states that the algebraic sum of potential differences around any closed loop must be zero, embodying conservation of energy[cite: 147].

questions.question: Three resistors of 10 Ω, 20 Ω, and 30 Ω are connected in series across a 12 V battery. What is the circuit current?
questions.explanation: Req = 10 + 20 + 30 = 60 Ω[cite: 148]. Current I = V / Req = 12 V / 60 Ω = 0.2 A[cite: 148].

questions.question: What is the magnetic force F⃗ on a charge q moving with velocity v⃗ in a magnetic field B⃗?
questions.explanation: The magnetic Lorentz force on a moving charge is F⃗ = q(v⃗ × B⃗) with magnitude F = qvB sin θ[cite: 150].

questions.question: What is the SI unit of magnetic field strength B?
questions.explanation: The SI unit for magnetic field strength B is the tesla (T); 1 T = 10⁴ gauss[cite: 151].

questions.question: How is magnetic flux Φ defined through a planar surface of area A oriented perpendicular to uniform magnetic field B?
questions.explanation: Magnetic flux is defined as Φ = B · A cos θ; when perpendicular, Φ = BA, measured in webers (Wb)[cite: 152, 153].

questions.question: Faraday's Law of Induction states that the magnitude of the induced emf in a coil of N turns is proportional to:
options: The time rate of change of magnetic flux (ε = -N ΔΦ / Δt)
The resistance of the wire turns
The electrostatic potential of the battery
questions.explanation: Faraday's law states that induced emf equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit: ε = -N(ΔΦ/Δt)[cite: 154].

questions.question: What is the forbidden energy band gap (Eg) in typical insulators compared to semiconductors?
options: Insulators have Eg < 1 eV; semiconductors have Eg > 10 eV
Insulators have a large forbidden gap (> 3 eV); semiconductors have a narrow gap (< 3 eV)
Conduction and valence bands overlap in insulators
questions.explanation: Insulators have large band gaps (> 3 eV, e.g., diamond is 6 eV), whereas semiconductors have gaps < 3 eV (silicon is 1.1 eV)[cite: 148, 149].

questions.question: What type of extrinsic semiconductor is produced when pure silicon is doped with a pentavalent impurity like arsenic (As)?
options: Intrinsic semiconductor with equal carrier densities
questions.explanation: Pentavalent impurities donate extra conduction electrons, creating an N-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers[cite: 151, 152].

questions.question: How must an external voltage source be connected to forward-bias a P-N junction diode?
options: Positive terminal to N-region; negative terminal to P-region
Positive terminal to P-region; negative terminal to N-region
Both terminals connected directly to the P-region
questions.explanation: In forward bias, the positive battery terminal connects to the P-side and the negative terminal to the N-side, narrowing the depletion layer[cite: 154, 155].

questions.question: What is the phase difference between input and output voltage signals in a common-emitter (CE) transistor amplifier?
questions.explanation: In common-emitter configuration, the output signal is 180° out of phase with the input signal (phase reversal)[cite: 160, 161].

questions.question: Which logic gate produces an output that is LOW (0) ONLY when both of its inputs are HIGH (1)?
questions.explanation: A NAND gate produces an output that is the inverse of an AND gate, giving 0 only when both inputs are 1[cite: 161].
